The z-Transform and its Region of Convergence (L07)

Why this matters in the exam: L07 has never been tested (Sample Test 1 covered only L02–L04), so it is a strong candidate for the final. Tutorial 6 is the only practice set, and its three questions match the likely exam pattern: find and sketch the ROC, use , and get from a block diagram and judge causality. Sample Test 1 split 20 marks into parts worth 4–7 marks, so expect a z-transform question of about 4–7 marks. Almost every later topic (L08 inverse transforms, stability, L09 filters) assumes you can do this quickly and without ROC mistakes.

1. The core ideas

1.1 Definition (L07 slide 4)

  • What it is: a power series in . The coefficient of is . So sits with , and sits with .
  • Why it matters for systems: feed into an LTI system and the output is with . So is the z-transform of the impulse response.
  • Trap: an answer is only complete with its ROC (L07 slide 6). alone does not fix . The pair is “ + ROC”.

1.2 The ROC (L07 slide 8)

The ROC is the set of where the sum converges. Convergence depends only on , so the ROC is always a ring centred on the origin.

Signal type Definition (L07 slide 7) ROC shape Sketch to draw
Finite length nonzero for finitely many whole plane, except possibly and/or shade everything; mark 0 or if excluded
Causal (right-sided) for outside a circle, (includes ) dashed circle through the outermost pole, shade outside
Anti-causal (left-sided) for inside a circle, dashed circle through the innermost pole, shade inside
Two-sided neither a ring , or empty two dashed circles, shade the annulus (see the figure in Example 2)

Two extra rules from L07 slide 17:

  • The ROC never contains a pole. It is bounded by poles (or by and ).
  • So for a rational the ROC boundaries are circles through pole radii. Draw the circles as dashed lines. The boundary itself is not in the ROC.

1.5 Rational : poles and zeros (L07 slides 16–17)

  • finite zeros (roots of the numerator) and finite poles (roots of the denominator).
  • The factor gives: zeros at if , or poles at if .
  • At infinity: a zero at if , a pole at if .
  • Counting check: including and , the number of poles equals the number of zeros.
  • Poles are drawn , zeros . Write the order beside a repeated one, for example “(2)”.
  • Trap: always multiply through to get polynomials in (positive powers) before reading off zeros and poles at the origin. Reading them from the form hides the ones at 0.

1.6 Interconnections (L03 slides 11–12, used in T6 Q3)

Each block multiplies in the z-domain, because convolution becomes multiplication.

Connection Time domain Transfer function
Cascade
Parallel (adder) (use the sign at the adder)
Negative feedback: forward , feedback , minus at adder
Positive feedback (plus at adder)

The feedback formula is not on the L07 slides. It comes from writing the adder equation , , and solving for . Do that derivation in the exam rather than quoting it, so the sign is right.

Is the result causal? A system is causal if for (L08 slide 8: ROC is the exterior of a circle, including ).

  • Causal blocks in cascade, parallel or feedback (with a delay in the loop) give a causal system.
  • One non-causal block (any positive power of , like in T6 Q3) usually makes the whole system non-causal. Check the final : expand it and look for any term (). Cancellations can occur, so do not decide from one block alone.
  • For a rational in positive powers of : causal is only possible if , so that is finite.

1.7 Link to the DTFT (L07 slide 5)

  • The DTFT is the z-transform evaluated on the unit circle, .
  • It exists only if the ROC contains the unit circle. Example: has ROC , which misses , so it has no DTFT.
  • Fast values: is , so . And is , so .
  • A zero on the unit circle at makes . A pole close to the circle makes a peak (L04/L09 pole-zero intuition).

2. The method

Recognising the question type. “Find the z-transform and sketch the ROC” means Playbook A. “Given of a known signal, find the transform of a modified signal” means Playbook B. “Compute the convolution using the z-transform” means Playbook C (and the inverse step is in D8). “Block diagram, transfer function, causal?” means Playbook D. “Poles and zeros” means Playbook E. “Frequency response / does the DTFT exist?” means Playbook F.

Playbook A: forward transform and ROC.

  1. Split into pieces: finite-length pieces, causal exponentials and anti-causal exponentials .
  2. Transform each piece from the table, keeping signs. Write each piece’s ROC next to it.
  3. Add the pieces (linearity). The ROC is the intersection of the piece ROCs.
  4. If the intersection is empty (for example and ), say “the z-transform does not exist”.
  5. Combine over a common denominator if asked, and write it as a polynomial ratio in (the course’s style in T6).
  6. Sketch: axes, unit circle (dotted), dashed circles at the boundary radii, pole marks, shade the ROC.

Playbook B: properties.

  1. Identify which operation was done to : shift, scale by , reverse, expand, multiply by , convolve.
  2. Apply the z-domain rule from the property table to the whole (substitute everywhere).
  3. Transform the ROC with the matching rule: shift keeps it (check 0 and ); scaling multiplies radii by ; reversal inverts radii and swaps inner and outer; expansion takes the -th root.
  4. If has a property-shaped form, such as , use the property instead of the definition sum.

Playbook C: convolution through the z-transform (T6 Q2).

  1. Find with ROC and with ROC (Playbook A).
  2. , ROC (or larger if a pole cancels).
  3. Inverse transform by partial fractions. Each pole is causal if the ROC is outside it, and anti-causal if the ROC is inside it (method in D8).

Playbook D: block diagram.

  1. Transform every block: an FIR becomes a polynomial. Find the arrow: the sample at multiplies , the sample at multiplies , the sample at multiplies .
  2. Label the signal after each adder. Write one equation per adder.
  3. Combine: cascade multiplies, parallel adds (with the adder sign), feedback solves .
  4. Simplify and, for FIR, expand to read straight off the coefficients.
  5. Causality: any () term left means , so not causal.

Playbook E: poles and zeros.

  1. Multiply top and bottom by the highest power of so both are polynomials in .
  2. Factor the numerator for zeros and the denominator for poles.
  3. Add any zeros or poles at from the leftover power of .
  4. Check : means a zero at ; means a pole at .
  5. Count: total poles = total zeros. If not, you have missed one at 0 or .

Playbook F: DTFT link.

  1. Check the ROC contains . If not, the DTFT does not exist.
  2. Substitute . For a single frequency, substitute the number: , , for .

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Giving with no ROC. This is half an answer. T6 Q1(a) and (b) have identical and differ only in the ROC.
  • Sign of the anti-causal pair. . So (T6 Q1(a)).
  • Shift direction. , not .
  • Time reversal ROC. Invert both radii and swap them: becomes (T6 Q1(d)). Writing again, or , loses the mark.
  • Missing poles or zeros at 0 and . Read them from the positive-power form and do the count check.
  • Using the initial value theorem on a non-causal signal. It only holds when for .
  • The arrow in FIR blocks. is . Dropping the hides the non-causality in T6 Q3.
  • Saying the DTFT is at when the ROC misses the unit circle. Check the ROC first.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

z-TRANSFORM (L07)   X(z) = sum x(k) z^-k ;  coeff of z^-n is x(n).  ALWAYS give ROC.
ROC: ring about 0, contains no poles, bounded by poles.
  finite: all z (drop 0 if n>0 samples, drop inf if n<0 samples)
  causal: |z| > outermost pole      anti-causal: |z| < innermost pole
  two-sided: ring between poles (empty -> no transform)
PAIRS: delta(n)->1 ; delta(n-d)->z^-d
  a^n u(n)       -> 1/(1-a z^-1), |z|>|a|
  -a^n u(-n-1)   -> 1/(1-a z^-1), |z|<|a|   (SAME X, different ROC; watch sign)
  n a^n u(n)     -> a z^-1/(1-a z^-1)^2, |z|>|a|
  a^n cos(w0 n)u(n) -> (1-a cos w0 z^-1)/(1-2a cos w0 z^-1+a^2 z^-2), |z|>|a|
PROPERTIES: x(n-d)->z^-d X (x(n+4)->z^4 X) ; z0^n x->X(z/z0), |z0|R
  e^{jw0 n}x -> X(e^{-jw0} z) ; x(-n)->X(1/z), radii inverted & swapped
  x_(k)(n)->X(z^k), R^(1/k) ; n x(n) -> -z dX/dz ; conv -> product, ROC >= Rx∩Rh
  IVT (causal only): x(0) = lim_{z->inf} X(z)
POLES/ZEROS: write in +ve powers of z. z^(N-M) factor -> zeros (N>M) or poles (M>N) at 0.
  X(inf)=0 -> zero at inf ; X(inf)=inf -> pole at inf. #poles = #zeros incl 0, inf.
BLOCKS: cascade H1H2 ; parallel H1±H2 ; feedback G/(1+GF) (minus at adder), G/(1-GF) (plus)
  Causal? expand final H(z): any z^{+k} term -> h(-k)≠0 -> NOT causal.
DTFT: X(w) = X(z) at z=e^{jw}, only if ROC contains |z|=1. X(0)=X(z=1), X(pi)=X(z=-1).
